description: Wednesday 8 July 2026 | Finance and Expenditure Committee Te Here ā Nuku (Nelson Tenths) Bill Te Here ā Nuku Trust Kerensa Johnston Jamie Tuuta Indigenous Data Authority Lisa Pizzoni The Outdoor Access Commission, Herenga a Nuku Aotearoa Doug Macredie, Pononga Whakatere, Strategic Relationships Manager Dr Lorraine Eade Hon Dr Nick Smith Gillian Wratt Craig Atkinson Arthur Phillips William Stafford Trust Joseph Stafford, Trustee Te Tiriti o Waitangi Marae Ngati Kawa Aramiha Taituha, Chairman, Te Tiriti o Waitangi Marae Riwai Morgan Whanau Trust Paul Morgan Jason Savage
descriptionSummary: Te Here ā Nuku (Nelson Tenths) Bill. Te Here ā Nuku Trust. Kerensa Johnston

chunks.text: Kerensa Johnson, I can see you, and Jamie Tuta. Tena koutou. Welcome. Just want to unmute your screen there. And we've actually got you for 20 minutes this morning, but we'll hand over to you for any opening comments or query- Ka pai... remarks.

Can you hear us? Yes. Thank you. Ka pai. E mihi ana ki a koe, e Te Tiamana. Koutou, e te komiti whiriwhiri. Ka nui ra o te mihi ki a koutou. Nō reira, tena koutou. Nei ra matou o Te Here Anuku. So thank you all. Thank you for the opportunity to present to you all this morning.

Alongside myself as the chair of Te Here Anuku Trust, I have fellow trustees, Kerensa Johnson and Jeremy Banks, and we also have our legal counsel, Horiana Owen-Easthope online. What we thought, Chair, is that with just some brief introductory comments, and probably the best use of time would be to take any questions that the committee might have.

And as you expect, we support this bill in its entirety, and we urge that it be passed before the 2026 general election, and that's consistent with the Crown's commitment under the resolution agreement that was signed in December. And I think just for context, as the committee will know, this bill is not about taking something from the public.

It is about finally returning trust land to its rightful trust while preserving public access, conservation outcomes, and practical relationships with agencies and communities where it has been agreed. In such places as Abel Tasman, these arrangements have been agreed, and we believe are generous, balanced, and firmly in the public interest as well as in the interests of Ngā Uri being the beneficiaries of Te Here Anuku.

But when we reflect on this particular kaupapa, it is about whenua, and it is about whakapapa. It's about our relationship and connection to place and to each other. And at the heart of this particular kaupapa is about restoring a trust that has existed since 1845 but was not properly recognized or managed by the Crown.

And so our tupuna have never given up on that promise, and this bill is the final legislative step to give practical effect to the resolution reached after many years of litigation, negotiation, and engagement. And I think with that opening, unless, Kerensa, there's anything you want to add?

Chair, I think it'll be just most useful to hand over for questions. But Kerensa, kei a koe? Hi. Tena tatou katoa. Tenei te mihi nui ki a koutou i te ata nei. Kia ora, everybody. And just first of all, an apology. Jeremy and I are stuck in transit as most people are today, so it's a little bit noisy where we are. But we're here.

And just to add to what Jamie has said, it's important just first of all, just to acknowledge our whanau who we know are watching online. We want to thank them all for their support, and we know that a number of them have made submissions in support of the bill, and so just acknowledge those of you who are watching with us online. And also to reiterate what Jamie has said.

Apologies. This is a really significant milestone for us, another, a step closer to the end of what's been over 17 years of litigation in the courts, hard-fought by the Crown. But certainly the last few months have been incredibly proactive and positive in terms of the bill that we have before us, which we are very confident about.

The bill doesn't attempt to solve every question with respect to the trust estate, and we've certainly done a lot of work over the last few months, meeting with people in our community and on the ground, knowing that there will be other matters that we will resolve together in the coming months and years. So perhaps I'll leave it there, given I'm competing with Air New Zealand, unless Jeremy wants to add just anything before we open for questions.

I guess just a quick brief reflection. Before we gathered for the first reading, it was great to have the opportunity to end what has been a very hard-fought process in a positive way, and so that's what we're really focused on at the moment, is what this enables for us, what this enables for our whanau, and what the future looks like. So I'll just leave it there, open for questions. Kia ora koutou.

Thank you all for your submissions and comments this morning. Really appreciate it. Now we've got a question from Steve Abel. Kia ora koutou. Yeah, it feels like a somewhat momentous process, this one, and long fought, and we acknowledge the many, many years of effort and sacrifice that has gone into getting to this point for you, for Te Here Anuku.

You express that you support the bill in full. What are the concerns that you have? What are the things that you look at in the bill and that gives you some pause for thought, that you would want us as a committee considering this to take into account as we consider it?

I think I'll provide some context and then maybe hand over to the team. I think the bill- Implements what was agreed in the resolution agreement. Mm-hmm. There are elements within the resolution agreement and also the bill that, as Carenza noted, require us to work alongside with others. And so whether that be the Tasman District Council, the Department of Conservation, and others.

So, we couldn't prescribe everything. And some might argue that prescription is something that we should do, but it does require us to work proactively and engage with key parties that are utilizing our land for public benefit and other uses. So I think there is a piece there that in the spirit of what we've negotiated through the resolution agreement and bill, requires all parties to come together in a spirit of cooperation, recognizing too the place of Te Here Angiku, ownership of land, and responsibilities to our broader

beneficiaries. I think probably just the piece is really around any sort of future consenting. There is significant change happening at the moment in terms of resource management, and other reform programs. But again, striking that balance that at a point in time should it be the desire of future trustees and beneficiaries to utilize land in a particular way, that there are those mechanisms and that ability to be able to do that.

And so I think those are two elements. Carenza, Huriana, anything else from you? Thanks, Jamie. And to add to that, I would say we do support the bill in its entirety. We've worked really hard over the last few months since the resolution agreement to make sure we're very comfortable with where it has landed.

I think if anything, we understand that through the select committee process, we may have the benefit of your thinking around any improvements to the bill. But in terms of the material decisions and the principles underpinning it, we are very comfortable that they reflect the resolution agreement, and the aspirations not only of Ngā Uri, but also of course the Crown in terms of that ongoing relationship.

Can I ask a sup on that, Mr. Chair? Yep. Yeah. Thank you very much for that. One of the things that seems notable, I suppose, is the extent of the obligation that you carry to maintain those relationships with the other interested parties, the Tasman District Council or DOC.

Should we have consideration of the burden that places on the trust, in terms of resources, in terms of costs, in terms of personnel? And obviously you've considered this and this is where it's got to, but is there anything that we should be thinking of in that space, or is it as it's currently described, satisfactory in so far as there's enough leeway for you to determine the terms of that relationship?

I think, well, to start with, it goes to Carenza's point, right? I think we've struck the right balance- Yeah given the time in which we've negotiated arrangements. The bill and the resolution agreement does rest on, as I said earlier, entering into positive relationships with the likes of Tasman District Council, the Department of Conservation.

On the Department of Conservation side, we've taken some time to work through kaupapa or relationship agreement, which considers things both at a governance, but more importantly at an operational level around striking the right balance between the responsibilities and obligations of each party in relation to those lands.

And we'll be working through the same with the Tasman District Council and a small part with the Nelson City Council around some of those areas that are currently controlled and managed by them. Thank you. We've got a question from Glen Bennett. Thanks so much, and thanks for giving us your time this morning.

Really supportive of the process. It feels like we're almost at the finish line, and there's been a little bit of noise around this. How can you, I guess, reassure people who are asking questions about this, "Be not afraid. This is a good step forward"? Yeah. I guess, one, we've always encouraged and invited others to understand the history and the context to this particular issue.

The fact that this process is very much about restoring land, that is land that always belonged to the trust. And it's righting a longstanding legal wrong. And so I think that's the starting point. In addition to that, there has been public commentary from the Mayor of Nelson and others, and we can talk about this quite openly, about alternative options in relation to trust land for the Abel Tasman National Park.

And I think it's just important that you as a committee and I think the broader public just recognize, I think, the balance that has been struck by the trust, and the generosity that the trust has shown to enable the arrangements for at least another 25 years for the park. That, in our minds, is a useful timeframe that enables us to sort of- You know, work with the department and others over that period of time. Current concessions continue with their terms, and we've got quite a detailed statutory and operational arrangements which I think strike the right balance

between providing public access, but also recognizing the fact that a portion of the park, and I say a portion, is now owned by the trust. And so, Karenza, anything else from you? I think the history of this issue is really important, which is, as Jamie talked about at the outset, a private law trust established in 1845.

But the bigger rationale behind that was, it was always about the shared prosperity of our families and the people and community of Nelson. So, the idea was that we would rise together and create this community together. And so for us as trustees, and I think as the beneficiaries, that is a really important principle that has underpinned all of the work we've done over the last few years, and that will absolutely continue.

We know how loved all of our special places are at home by all of us. We care about those places as much as everybody else does, and we're not going anywhere. So, we feel very confident, comfortable that care will be taken with respect to all the decisions that we have to make, and that we'll do that with our community.

And just thinking ahead to what you'll be listening to through the course of the morning, some of the matters that have been raised in other submissions are, in our view, not appropriate for legislation or for the bill. They will be addressed, as Jamie has said, through our relationships.

Thank you. Dan Bidois. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Kia ora, Jamie, and to you as well, Karenza. This is actually just a supplementary on the previous question. As you've correctly pointed out, there have been concerns raised with other submissions around access and protection of the park. So, I guess, in a nutshell, what would you say to those that are concerned about future access and protection of the coastal areas of the Abel Tasman National Park? What do you say to those particular people today?

Well, I think as Karenza sort of just put it, people shouldn't be afraid. And this is something that we've shared directly with the Mayor of Nelson, former member of Parliament, is that we care deeply about these places. I think the generosity that has been shown by the trust is one where we've developed a mechanism, and we have certainty in relation to the Abel Tasman for the next 25 years, to ensure that public access is maintained and that special place is protected. People would say, "Well, actually, what's going to happen once that 25-year period sort of ends?"

And the message that we've given to everyone is we've got time to work through what the opportunities might be for that special place, and that's something that we'll continue to discuss and work through over the coming years. And I think what people should have confidence in is that we are deeply connected to this place.

Our name, Hereanuku, really speaks to the fact that this whole process has been very much about the restoration of whenua, the restoration of land, which we hold dearly. Because there are some saying, "Oh, the trust will sell off this land for millions of dollars," and all of these sorts of things, the typical scaremongering.

But all we would say is that we are deeply tied and connected to these places, and we will ensure that they are protected, not only for this generation, but future generations. Thank you. Dr. David Wilson, got a question there. You're on mute, sir.

Thank you, Jamie, for that answer. I think you may have actually answered my question. You mentioned there are some things on the horizon, such as RMA, and you did also mention changes of use that may be into the future. So I think, in some ways, through the development of this bill, there's some certainty there and some clarity there as to what might happen post 25 years or in the intervening years where we can work together.

I've seen many fabulous examples of that. So hopefully, in the spirit of the conversation, that will continue. Most definitely, and I think it goes back to Karenza's comments earlier. When this trust was established, and if you go back to the initial terms of the trust and the principles that underpinned it, it was very much to be an endowment for the benefit not only of the beneficiaries, but actually for the region as a whole.

And we've been at pains to sort of just remind the families and the wider community into Taiihu that this entity has a role to play in contributing not only to our beneficiaries, but to the broader region. And I think that's the piece that we're excited about, and I think it's the piece that people shouldn't lose sight of.

It's interesting, we've had comments now of just sort of who have said, "Oh, we'd prefer you to own and operate the park than others." But hey, we're just sort of really happy that we've managed to sort of land in a place which we think balances all interests and gives certainty Yeah, thanks, Jamie. Look, we have met time for your submission this morning, but I think the committee really enjoyed hearing from you.

And certainly, we can see a real joy that's beginning to come across as we take this to the final stages, hopefully within the next couple of months. So thanks again. Kia ora, Dante. Kia ora. Kia ora. Members, we've now got the Indigenous Data Authority.

Lisa Pisoni, I believe, is joining us, and as an organization has up to 10 minutes with us. Yep, are you there, Lisa? Can you hear me? Yes, we can. We're in your hands. Oh, cool. For some reason I can't hear you. That's okay. All right. Kia ora. Kia ora koutou. My name is Lisa Pisoni, and I am the founder and lead architect of the Indigenous Data Authority- Lisa, your sound's coming through-- Lisa?

Which is- Lisa?... an Indigenous-owned, Māori-owned and led charitable trust that works to operationalize Indigenous governance and practice. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today. First and foremost, I'd like to say that I support this bill. To me, this bill is not simply about returning land. It's about restoring authority.

The Nelson teens were never intended to be Crown land. They were intended to remain under Māori ownership, with the Crown acting as trustee. That promise has not been honored, and generations have now lived-... with those consequences. What this bill does-... is quite significant because it recognizes that distinction. It transfers legal title from Crown to former trustee, as former trustee to Te Henui Anuku Trust, while recognizing that beneficial ownership has always remained with the original customary owners, and creates a framework that

restores authority while recognizing that public conservation management and public access will continue. That distinction- Lisa, can you hear? Lisa?... is because governance and authority- Lisa? Lisa? Sorry, your sound's not very clear. Oh, wait.

Your sound's not very clear. Governance is how decisions are made, and authority is who has the legitimate right to make those decisions. Chair, would Liam have her contact number and maybe give her a call? That principle applies whether we are talking about Whenua Wai Taonga data or artificial intelligence.

My professional work focuses on governance systems, and regardless of the subject, the first question always needs to be the same. Who has legitimate authority to decide? To me, this bill begins to answer that question. One of the strengths of this legislation is that it does not present Māori authority and public administration as opposing concepts. Instead, it creates a practical governance model where both have a role to play. The Department of Conservation, local authorities, and other public agencies will continue to have important

statutory responsibilities. At the same time, Te Henui Anuku Trust will hold the legal authority of the trustee on behalf of the beneficial owners. That shouldn't be seen as a source of concern. It should be recognized as an opportunity to strengthen governance. For generations, Māori have exercised stewardship of these lands and waters through whakapapa, tikanga, and intergenerational knowledge.

That knowledge has sustained these spaces long before modern government agencies existed. Bringing that knowledge together with the statutory responsibility of public institutions creates a stronger foundation for decision-making rather than the being able to make them alone. Good governance is not about replacing one system with another. It is about ensuring that every organization exercises its responsibility within the limits of its legitimate authority while working together in the interests of both the whenua and the wider public,

which is also consistent with our constitutional foundations. Article 2 of Te Tiriti o Waitangi guarantees the continued exercise of tino rangatiratanga over lands, kaimoana, and taonga. While this bill cannot undo generations of loss, it recognizes that the authority over the whenua should sit with those who hold enduring whakapapa connections to it.

It is equally consistent with the United Nations Declarations on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, which recognizes, of course, the rights of Indigenous peoples to maintain and strengthen their relationship with their traditional lands, territories, and resources and to maintain- Liam, do we have an update on contacting Lisa? These principles are increasingly recognized around the world because good governance begins with legitimate authority.

My only recommendation is that this bill is implemented. The authority of the beneficial owners remains central to every decision made under it. Restoring legal title is important. Restoring genuine decision-making authority is essential. Finally, I hope Parliament sees this bill as more than just a resolution of a historical grievance.

I hope it's recognized as a contemporary example of good governance. When Parliament is considering Whenua Wai, natural resources, data, artificial intelligence, or any other taonga, the first question should never be, "How do we govern this?" The first question should always be, "Who holds the legitimate authority?" Because when authority sits with the right people, governance becomes legitimate.

And when authority is removed, governance becomes administrative. That, to me, is what this bill begins to correct, and for that reason, I support the bill. Ngā mihi nui Kia ora, Lisa. Can you hear me okay? Can you hear me at all? I can't hear you for some reason.

Can you take these out? Can you hear me now through your computer? Yeah. What about now? Way better. Sorry. A lot of your presentation was a little bit distorted, but we have got your- Oh, was it? We've got your written submission. Okay. And you're welcome to submit a further summary of what you spoke about.

But I don't know if committee members have any key questions. Probably just your last two sentences in summary would be really helpful, if you could just repeat those. So, basically it talks about the question should never be, how do we govern this?

It should be, who holds legitimate authority? And it should always go to those people who whakapapa to the whenua. Because when authority sits with the right people, governance becomes legitimate, and when authority is removed, governance becomes administrative.

Yeah. Thank you. And I think this bill addresses that. Very good. We've got a question from Dr. David Wilson, probably just- Yes, I think I got the gist that you're in favor of the bill, with some, should we say, some concerns. But I missed the bit that you talked about in terms of AI.

Are you worried about data sovereignty there? So it's about authority. So obviously data sovereignty, sovereignty, governance, it all ties together. It all fits together. And part of what I do is I push for indigenous authority. And speaking to this, it's about the authority and the legitimate authority of who should be making decisions or who should be a part of the decision-making process.

And that's why I support this bill. And can you relate what you just said to your point on AI for me? It's just given as an example. Because even with AI, we as the tangata whenua should have authority over anything related to us. Yeah. Thank you.
Okay. Thank you, Lisa. We have met time. Appreciate your submission today. Kia ora. We're now going to go to Doug and Maryanne from the Outdoor Access Commission.

Kia ora koutou. Kia ora, Doug. We've got you for 10 minutes, so we're in your hands. You're welcome to make some opening comments and then leave some time for questions. Kia ora. Tuatahi, e mihi ana ki te kaihanga, nana nei ngā mea katoa. Tuarua, ki a rātou katoa, ngā mātua tupuna kua wehe atu ki te po, haere jure, haere e oki.

Tuatoru, ki a tātou katoa ngā kanohi ora. Tuatahi ki te mana whenua o Te Tauihu, tēnā rawa atu koutou i roto i tēnei kaupapa whakahirahira me tēnei rā. Ki a koutou hoki, te komiti whakahaere o tēnei wāhanga o te kaupapa, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou.

Otirā, ki ngā tangata katoa o te whenua e whakarongo ana ki ēnei kōrero, tēnā rawa atu tātou katoa, Aotearoa whānui. Here Anuku, the Outdoor Access Commission, is the Crown agent responsible for public access to the outdoors. We are established under the Walking Access Act 2008, and our job is to advise on and advocate for free, certain, enduring, and practical access on foot, bike, horseback, or any other method for the many, many purposes that we all enjoy as New Zealanders in our beautiful country in the outdoors.

And we should note that we are all the public, regardless of race, background, age, gender, origin. And we should also note that public space is a wonderful place where we all get to share our cultures and being one another, including our mana whenuatanga, tanga, for tangata whenua.

We have a national network of regional field advisors. We map public access across the country and we're the agency people and other agencies do and should come to when a change of land affects how the public can move through it. That is why a title transfer of this scale sits squarely within our mandate.

The Commission supports the broad direction of the bill. The Nelson Tents case is one of the longest running property disputes in the history of Aotearoa, and transferring and correcting legal title to Here Anuku Trust as kaitiaki on behalf of owners is a significant step for all of Aotearoa.

We also welcome the initial protections for public access and recreation, and we note that in our experience, mana whenua and tangata whenua leadership in outdoor access is most usually, if not always, a strength. Correcting an ownership title of this scale will likely in places mean a change to the public access Both actual and potential. This is an expected consequence of correcting the historic title, and it is not in itself something that we oppose.

There are many examples where public access is actually improved by unformed legal road stoppings, as one example, whereby in those cases better alternatives are put in place, or where ULRs were actually of no relevance or interest to anybody.

The Outdoor Access Commission is taking a forward-looking stance with relation to the bill moving forward. Once the bill has passed and the title has transferred, we're asking for the opportunity to sit down with Te Here Anuku Trust, for open blue skies without prejudice conversation and dialogue about the future of public access.

We've found in our experience that outdoor access is best managed and improved and enhanced when all parties think from a blue skies approach, and we allow opportunities to eventuate in a proactive relationship. We're not asking the committee to change the bill.

We're asking it to note in its report support for this engagement process to take place. Please note that given the select committee time frames, we haven't had the chance to analyze the unformed legal road and land parcels involved for their public access value, and that is a gap.

Had we been brought into the conversation earlier, we could have provided useful supportive background before the bill was drafted, not to slow it down, but to help get the access settings right from the start. That's part of why we're asking to be part of the conversation moving forward. To sum up, we support the bill's broad direction.

We understand that some changes to practical access are expected as part of the righting of this historic wrong, and our one substantive ask is for the committee's in-principle support for an ongoing constructive relationship between Te Here Anuku Trust and the Outdoor Access Commission.

Public access matters for connection to whenua for all, for enriching our collective wairua as a country, and for improving our biodiversity and to the people who use it every day. We want to keep being the voice that represents that interest and be at the table.

Kia ora. Thank you, Doug. First question is from Dan Rosewarne. Yeah, thanks Chair, and thanks Doug for that contribution. You kind of half answered my question, but I just want to clarify. So you mentioned around Clause 116 to stop unformed legal roads, and noting that you haven't had a lot of consideration time. I was just wondering, are there any particular examples around these parcels of land that stick out for you that we should be aware of?

I might defer to my colleague, Marianne, and just give a quick general comment. When we look at unformed legal roads, we look at both the current use, which sometimes is nothing, sometimes is something, but also the future and potential use. So it's quite an involved process, but I hope Marianne is here as well.

Yeah. Kia ora, Marianne. Kia ora, Doug. Yeah, pretty much we haven't had time to fully analyze all the particular parcels involved. We note that some are actually mentioned in the bill, then the schedules also have included mention of other ones in Milnethorpe.

We're just conscious that even though vehicles mightn't use these, the public still have the right to use them, and a lot of the public do use them for walking and cycle ways. And we're aware of a lot of projects for outdoor access that are happening in the Golden Bay area in particular that have identified unformed legal roads to get off-road access for cycle ways and walking.

So we're just conscious that they are included in the bill. And yes, we'd like the ability to be able to have further discussions involving any of those. Thanks, Marianne. Thank you. Steve Abel. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you Doug and Marianne. I'm wondering, your key point is that you'd like the opportunity to have that conversation with Te Here Anuku.

I'm not sure if it's the committee's place to intervene in that relationship, and I'm concerned that it seems that-- I presume you will have reached out to them already, and that that is a matter between the Outdoor Access Walking Trust and Te Here Anuku.

And I wonder, I'm not convinced that it's something for the committee to be making a comment on, really. I think it's implicit in the assumption of the responsibility that Te Here Anuku has that they need to be the one that's approached as the authority holder.

Okay. If that is in fact the case, I think it's still been a fabulous opportunity to express our stance in terms of looking forward positively, fully acknowledging the transfer and the correcting of the title to the mana whenua, and also acknowledging and putting forward the point that we are all members of the public. Mana whenua, nga tangata katoa o Aotearoa. But, uh, tena koe mo to-- mo tena whakaaro.

Kia ora. And we absolutely admire the work you do, and no way questioning the huge value of it and the essence of what you represent as a principle of access. So kia ora. Kia ora, Steve. Thank you, Doug, and for your organization and colleague online.

We have met time, so appreciate your submission today. Kia ora. Kia ora. Kia ora. Thank you. Members, we're going to go to Dr. Lorraine Eade, who's making a personal submission. Are you there, Dr. Lorraine? Kia ora. Kia ora. Can you hear me? Kia ora. Yes. We've only got you for five minutes, so I encourage you to largely take your submission as read to allow time for questions.

Ka pai. So first of all, I just want to acknowledge Uncle Pat, Uncle Rory Stafford, for over 40 years of leadership around Y56 and this private law case. That's a heavy load for anyone to carry, so just want to acknowledge and honor him. Just in terms of the Spain Award, of the 151,000 odd acres, 69,000 entitlement of those acres were set for Ngati Rarua and Takaka, Mutapi, Mutuika, and Motiri.

So that 69,000 acres equates to just 45.746%. The crux of my submission is around the decision of August 2023 to allow other uri, other iwi, into the Nelson tents case. So there were 254 tupuna that were listed in the original Native Land Court hearing.

Now, in terms of that, they followed due process through the Native Land Court, and Ngati Rarua, Te Atiawa, Ngati Tama, and Ngati Koata were identified as owners of the Nelson tents. A decision was made overnight to include other tupuna without coming back to the descendants of those original 254 tupuna.

That's basically the crux of the submission. It's another injustice on top of injustice over the last 181 years. In terms of the lands, the treaty settlement process that we've gone through, Ngati Rarua also included the Nelson tents in their claim, and this seems like an injustice to Ngati Rarua, who had the majority of land share ownings, and now we have other owners in there.

One of the things that we would like to see, and you can see there's some signatories in there. Just for your information, Eru Kipa has withdrawn his signature from the petition. He didn't quite read it 100%, so he has withdrawn. So there's 19 people who have supported the submission as to go through the Maori Land Court process in terms of determining who are the customary owners of those lands. Now, we have been through a number of processes, and signaled this at AGMs, at Te Hiri Nuku

open hui, and we've got nowhere, really. So this is predominantly the last opportunity to have it on record. No matter what happens, at least I can tell my mokopuna when they come to challenge in two generations' time, that this was put forward. So kia ora.

I think I've got a minute left. You have. Yeah. Thank you for your submission. Obviously, you stood up and shared these concerns during the process with Te Hiri Nuku. What was their response to some of your concerns? That it was an overnight decision.

It was at the remedies hearing. Evidence was going to be given the next day, and advice was provided. They were between a rock and a hard place. Advice was provided, and an agreement was made. Now, we've never seen that agreement, but obviously there are another tupuna, there are other owners in Te Hiri Nuku. And just in terms of equity and justice, think that that needs to go back through the Maori Land Court, who determined who the original owners were in 1892.

Very good. All right. Well, we- So we've not got very far, is what I'm saying. Thank you. Appreciate your submission, and you certainly discharged your obligations to do everything in your power. So acknowledge the work you've done there. Kia ora. Kia ora. Members, we're now going to welcome Dr. Nick Smith. Kia ora.

This is also in a personal capacity Dr Nick, are you there? I indeed am. Kia ora to yourself, Ryan, and to members of the Select Committee. Really appreciate the opportunity to be able to make a submission. This is a hugely significant bill for the Nelson and Tasman communities, and my submission is particularly focused on one of our gems, the Abel Tasman National Park. There has not been the time for either of our councils, with the list of properties affected only becoming public a bit over a week ago, for our councils to make submissions,

so this is in my own role individually, albeit I note over 1,800 people have signed a petition with similar concerns to mine with respect to the Abel Tasman National Park. I emphasize that I do not question the need to resolve the Nelson tents issue. My concern is that we are not going to get the best outcome for our region or for the new Te Hārihi Nuku Trust and its beneficial owners due to the rushed process and the lack of community engagement, both on the deed and this bill.
